item.text: {"text":"Activation patching identifies effects under a particular intervention; it does not automatically reveal a natural history-content pathway. [Zhang and Nanda (ICLR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042) show that corruption methods and evaluation metrics can substantially change localization. Prefer matched natural replacements and score margins over relying solely on Gaussian corruption or saturated probabilities. Natural donors still cannot guarantee that the resulting hybrid activation is on-distribution. [Makelov et al. (ICLR 2024)](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/70b8505ac79e3e131756f793cd80eb8d-Abstract-Conference.html) demonstrate that successful subspace interventions can activate dormant pathways, producing misleading localization. [Mueller (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04690) further explains how redundant causes and nontransitive counterfactual dependencies undermine simple circuit interpretations.\n\nFor the frozen BERT4Rec experiment, a defensible adaptation is to construct paired training histories matched on length, padding, popularity and recency while varying the hypothesized content; keep the appended mask and candidate set fixed. Test both restoration and disruption, reporting raw target-versus-alternative score changes alongside normalized recovery. Include identity patches, matched donors preserving the relevant content, unrelated donors, and random sites matched in intervention size. Treat activation norms or distribution distances as artifact diagnostics, not proof of validity. Select sites on discovery prefixes, then freeze hypotheses and confirm effects on unused training prefixes, preferably from disjoint users, with user-level uncertainty and multiple-comparison correction. These are proposed safeguards rather than established recommender-specific guarantees. [Shi et al. (NeurIPS 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13032) provide formal tests of circuit preservation, localization and minimality. All probes can operate within the single frozen category model, without additional predictors or test-label access."}
